item.title: What does the Myanmar genocide ruling mean for the Rohingya?
item.description:
Fleeing violence and persecution, Rohingya refugees walk after crossing the Naf River from Myanmar into Bangladesh on Oct. 9, 2017. Photo by Fred Dufour/AFP via Getty Images In a 9-6 vote, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in the northern Rakhine State. This is a remarkable moment for the Rohingya people and international justice – the first time, in fact, that the ICJ has ever ruled that a state committed this crime. It is a historic victory, worthy of celebration in a world where good things happen all too sparsely. Especially because it is a victory won against a global legal architecture almost designed to never find that a state committed genocide. item.title: Rohingya genocide survivor: ‘perpetrators will have to face consequences’
item.description:
Erin Ogunkeye welcomes Reed Brody, Member of the International Commission of Jurists, Human Rights Lawyer and veteran war crimes prosecutor. The International Court of Justice's ruling on Myanmar marks, according to Brody, "a historic victory for the Rohingya, but also a landmark for international justice." He explains how the court assessed evidence of genocidal intent, rejecting Myanmar's justification of its military operations as counterterrorism. He argues that "the existence of an armed conflict or a security objective doesn't exclude genocidal intent," a finding he believes will have "far-reaching implications in future genocide cases," including South Africa's case against Israel over Gaza. Brody also discusses the Gambia's role in bringing the case and growing challenges to international accountability, warning that "we're in a very dangerous moment."

item.title: Trump, Xi, Putin summit: What was it all about?
item.description:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up? That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday. It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse. item.title: NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from record one light-day away, 49 years after launch
item.description:
This illustration shows Voyager 1 passing by the rings of Saturn. NASA/Hulton Archive/Getty Images In the summer of 2027, the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft will each reach a milestone in time. On Sept. 5 and Aug. 20, respectively, they will each have spent 50 years in space . During their journeys, they first explored the planets of the outer solar system, then traveled to the edge of the solar system. Eventually, they passed into the interstellar medium : the space between stars. Although not the first spacecraft ever launched, these are now the two oldest spacecraft still operating. But before the spacecraft hit their semicentennial, Voyager 1 will also reach a milestone in distance. item.title: Investors scramble for a piece of AI giant Anthropic in blockbuster IPO
item.description:
Anthropic on Wednesday priced its initial public offering at $83 a share , above the price range the startup initially set, as the company’s highly anticipated debut tests the appetite for the AI trade. The higher-than-expected price demonstrated that investor enthusiasm for the first frontier lab to IPO has weathered turmoil in tech stocks following a Democratic midterms sweep and Jensen Huang’s ouster as Nvidia CEO, and that investors differentiate Anthropic as a pure-play AI company, as sentiment cools on AI infrastructure and hardware . The debut could draw about $250 million in net retail buying — potentially twice as much as SpaceX’s record of $118 million in retail buying . — Brendan Ruberry

item.title: Iowans brace for lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals
item.description:
When the U.S. Army blows up nearly five tons of unstable lead azide in southeastern Iowa on Friday, blanketing communities in lead-containing particles up to 100 miles away, it has a simple solution for concerned Iowans: Just rinse it off. “The good thing is, if people have concerns about it being on their property, all they have to do is hose that off, and it’s gone,” Army spokesperson Justine Barati told Radio Iowa earlier this week. This won’t be sufficient to mitigate the harm of the toxic plume the Army plans to release, environmental health experts based in Iowa told The Intercept. item.title: Venezuela signs military deal with US less than a year after Maduro's removal
item.description:
Nils Eekhoff is heading to Decathlon-CMA CGM after a decade with the Picnic-PostNL organization, first with the development team and then, for the past seven years, at the WorldTour level. The 28-year-old Dutchman was a promising prospect, having won the under-23 Paris-Roubaix race back in 2017 and having crossed the finish line first in the U23 road race at Yorkshire Worlds in 2019 before he was disqualified for spending too much time drafting a car after a crash. His biggest win as a pro came at Nokere Koerse last year. "He will help strengthen our sprint train, while also supporting our ambitions in stage races," said Romain Bardet, who will be Decathlon's sports manager in 2027. "We also hope to continue developing his potential in the spring classics, where he possesses all the qualities needed to support our collective goals.”
